claim: The adult human visual system maintains the ability to be altered by sensory deprivation.
source: The adult human visual system maintains the ability to be altered by sensory deprivation.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Internal neural states influence baseline contrast sensitivity.
source: The results demonstrate that internal neural states influence not only baseline contrast sensitivity but also the extent to which the adult visual system can undergo changes in ocular dominance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differences in contrast sensitivity between PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: Internal neural states influence the extent to which the adult visual system can undergo changes in ocular dominance.
source: The results demonstrate that internal neural states influence not only baseline contrast sensitivity but also the extent to which the adult visual system can undergo changes in ocular dominance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differences in ocular dominance shifts between PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation (30 min to 2.5 hr) results in changes in visual sensitivity.
source: Recent studies have shown that when one eye is deprived of its input for a short period of time (30 min to 2.5 hr), visual brain mechanisms undergo a neural change that results in not only a change in visual sensitivity but also interocular balance (i.e., ocular dominance) (Lunghi et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation (30 min to 2.5 hr) results in changes in interocular balance (ocular dominance).
source: Recent studies have shown that when one eye is deprived of its input for a short period of time (30 min to 2.5 hr), visual brain mechanisms undergo a neural change that results in not only a change in visual sensitivity but also interocular balance (i.e., ocular dominance) (Lunghi et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation effects peak immediately after patch removal.
source: However, unlike the long-term neuroplastic changes by abnormal visual experience in critical period, such change peaks immediately after patch removal and remains for up to 30–90 min (Lunghi et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013a), which we call as short-term monocular deprivation effect.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation effects remain for up to 30-90 min after patch removal.
source: However, unlike the long-term neuroplastic changes by abnormal visual experience in critical period, such change peaks immediately after patch removal and remains for up to 30–90 min (Lunghi et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013a), which we call as short-term monocular deprivation effect.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation effects mainly involve V1 (the primary visual cortex).
source: A number of results suggest that this short-term monocular deprivation effect mainly involves V1 (the primary visual cortex), these include intrinsic optical imaging in monkeys (Begum and Tso, 2015), and magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies (Chadnova et al., 2017), electroencephalogram (EEG) studies (Lunghi et al., 2015a; Zhou et al., 2015), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies (Binda et al., 2018), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) studies (Lunghi et al., 2015b) and psychophysics studies (Zhou et al., 2014) in human adults.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies using different methodologies.

claim: There is a significant decrease in occipital alpha oscillations when two eyes are open vs. closed in the dark, called the Berger effect.
source: It is well known that there are characteristic differences in resting-state brain activity in the absence of visual stimulation, for example, when the two eyes are open vs. closed in the dark, there is a significant decrease in occipital alpha oscillations called the Berger effect.
evidence: This is stated as well-known scientific knowledge.

claim: There are power and coherence changes across multiple frequency bands (Δ, θ, α1, α2, β1, β2, and γ) when eyes are open vs. closed.
source: There are power and coherence changes of a broad spectrum in the Δ, θ, α1, α2, β1, β2, and γ frequency bands that are presumed to be correlates of the switching of involuntary preliminary attention from internally directed attention specific for the eyes closed state to externally directed attention specific for the eyes open state (Boytsova and Danko, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Eyes open rest conditions are associated with larger activation of the visual cortex compared to eyes closed conditions.
source: FMRI studies have shown that eyes open rest conditions are associated with larger activation of the visual cortex but smaller activation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (Marx et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to fMRI study.

claim: Eyes open rest conditions are associated with smaller activation of the lateral geniculate nucleus compared to eyes closed conditions.
source: FMRI studies have shown that eyes open rest conditions are associated with larger activation of the visual cortex but smaller activation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (Marx et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to fMRI study.

claim: In the eyes closed state, activations of ocular motor-related brain areas are larger, including the prefrontal eye fields, parietal and frontal eye fields, cerebellar vermis, thalamus, and basal ganglia.
source: In the eyes closed state, activations of the ocular motor-related brain areas are larger, including the prefrontal eye fields, parietal and frontal eye fields, cerebellar vermis, thalamus, and basal ganglia (Marx et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Eye closure can alter the processing mode of the sensory system by decoupling geniculostriate processing in favor of enhanced thalamocortical coupling in non-visual brain areas.
source: It has been argued that eye closure can alter the processing mode of the sensory system by decoupling geniculostriate processing in favor of enhanced thalamocortical coupling in non-visual brain areas (Brodoehl et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Alpha amplitude was significantly lower when two eyes are open compared to closed (t(19) = –2.272, p=0.035).
source: Similar to previous reports (Boytsova and Danko, 2010), alpha amplitude was significantly lower when two eyes are open compared to closed (t(19) = –2.272, p=0.035, two-tailed paired samples t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979), number of comparisons k=2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In monocular patching conditions, alpha amplitude was significantly lower when the PE remained open compared to when the PE was kept closed (t(19) = –3.944, p<0.001).
source: Importantly, in the monocular patching conditions, the alpha amplitude was significantly lower when the PE remaining open as compared to the PE being kept closed (t(19) = –3.944, p<0.001, with Holm-Bonferroni correction, k=2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SSVEP amplitude was stronger for the PE-open condition compared with the PE-closed condition (t(19) = 2.737, p=0.026).
source: The results in Figure 1c show stronger SSVEP (t(19) = 2.737, p=0.026, with Holm-Bonferroni correction, k=2) and weaker alpha oscillations (t(19) = –2.683, p=0.015, with Holm-Bonferroni correction, k=2) for the PE-open condition compared with the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Alpha oscillations were weaker for the PE-open condition compared with the PE-closed condition (t(19) = –2.683, p=0.015).
source: The results in Figure 1c show stronger SSVEP (t(19) = 2.737, p=0.026, with Holm-Bonferroni correction, k=2) and weaker alpha oscillations (t(19) = –2.683, p=0.015, with Holm-Bonferroni correction, k=2) for the PE-open condition compared with the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The contrast sensitivity of the UPE with PE open was higher than that with PE closed (t(17) = 2.667, p=0.016).
source: As shown by Figure 1d, the contrast sensitivity of the UPE with PE open was also higher than that with PE closed (t(17) = 2.667, p=0.016).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Contrast sensitivity of the UPE was immediately decreased by 7.5% in the PE-closed condition compared to PE-open condition.
source: Compared to the PE condition, the contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude of the UPE were immediately decreased by 7.5% and 12.3%, whereas the amplitudes of αSSVEP, αBi, and αmono were immediately enhanced by 18.1%, 6.2%, and 23.3%, respectively, in the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: SSVEP amplitude of the UPE was immediately decreased by 12.3% in the PE-closed condition compared to PE-open condition.
source: Compared to the PE condition, the contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude of the UPE were immediately decreased by 7.5% and 12.3%, whereas the amplitudes of αSSVEP, αBi, and αmono were immediately enhanced by 18.1%, 6.2%, and 23.3%, respectively, in the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: Peak alpha amplitude in SSVEP sessions (αSSVEP) was immediately enhanced by 18.1% in the PE-closed condition compared to PE-open condition.
source: Compared to the PE condition, the contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude of the UPE were immediately decreased by 7.5% and 12.3%, whereas the amplitudes of αSSVEP, αBi, and αmono were immediately enhanced by 18.1%, 6.2%, and 23.3%, respectively, in the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: Peak alpha amplitude in resting state with both eyes open/closed (αBi) was immediately enhanced by 6.2% in the PE-closed condition compared to PE-open condition.
source: Compared to the PE condition, the contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude of the UPE were immediately decreased by 7.5% and 12.3%, whereas the amplitudes of αSSVEP, αBi, and αmono were immediately enhanced by 18.1%, 6.2%, and 23.3%, respectively, in the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: Peak alpha amplitude in resting state with PE open/closed (αmono) was immediately enhanced by 23.3% in the PE-closed condition compared to PE-open condition.
source: Compared to the PE condition, the contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude of the UPE were immediately decreased by 7.5% and 12.3%, whereas the amplitudes of αSSVEP, αBi, and αmono were immediately enhanced by 18.1%, 6.2%, and 23.3%, respectively, in the PE-closed condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: A positive correlation exists between the effect of eye open vs. eye close on contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude (r=0.665, p=0.013).
source: As shown in Figure 2, a positive correlation of the effect of eye open vs. eye close was found between contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude (r=0.665, p=0.013), and between peak alpha amplitudes in the SSVEP sessions and resting state (αSSVEP vs. αBi: r=0.558, p=0.011; αSSVEP vs. αmono: r=0.643, p=0.002; αBi vs. αmono: r=0.468, p=0.037).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A positive correlation exists between peak alpha amplitudes in SSVEP sessions and resting state with both eyes open/closed (αSSVEP vs. αBi: r=0.558, p=0.011).
source: As shown in Figure 2, a positive correlation of the effect of eye open vs. eye close was found between contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude (r=0.665, p=0.013), and between peak alpha amplitudes in the SSVEP sessions and resting state (αSSVEP vs. αBi: r=0.558, p=0.011; αSSVEP vs. αmono: r=0.643, p=0.002; αBi vs. αmono: r=0.468, p=0.037).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A positive correlation exists between peak alpha amplitudes in SSVEP sessions and resting state with PE open/closed (αSSVEP vs. αmono: r=0.643, p=0.002).
source: As shown in Figure 2, a positive correlation of the effect of eye open vs. eye close was found between contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude (r=0.665, p=0.013), and between peak alpha amplitudes in the SSVEP sessions and resting state (αSSVEP vs. αBi: r=0.558, p=0.011; αSSVEP vs. αmono: r=0.643, p=0.002; αBi vs. αmono: r=0.468, p=0.037).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: A positive correlation exists between peak alpha amplitudes in resting state with both eyes open/closed and PE open/closed (αBi vs. αmono: r=0.468, p=0.037).
source: As shown in Figure 2, a positive correlation of the effect of eye open vs. eye close was found between contrast sensitivity and SSVEP amplitude (r=0.665, p=0.013), and between peak alpha amplitudes in the SSVEP sessions and resting state (αSSVEP vs. αBi: r=0.558, p=0.011; αSSVEP vs. αmono: r=0.643, p=0.002; αBi vs. αmono: r=0.468, p=0.037).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, the contrast sensitivity of the UPE decreased by 32.1%.
source: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, the contrast sensitivity of the UPE changed from 103.086±6.961 (mean ± SE) before patching to 70.017±6.236 immediately after removal of the patch. This means that the short-term monocular deprivation temporally decreased the contrast sensitivity of the UPE by 32.1%.
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements before and after patching.

claim: The aftereffect of 2.5 hr of monocular patching on monocular contrast sensitivity was 34.5% less in the PE-closed condition than in the PE-open condition.
source: In contrast, the contrast sensitivity of the UPE decreased from 90.324±6.791 to 69.324±4.685 after 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-closed condition. This implies that the aftereffect of 2.5 hr of monocular patching on monocular contrast sensitivity was 34.5% less in the PE-closed condition than that in the PE-open condition.
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements comparing PE-open and PE-closed conditions.

claim: The contrast sensitivity of the UPE becomes smaller after 2.5 hr of monocular patching for both eye-closed patching (F(2,22) = 17.213, p<0.001, partial η2=0.610) and eye-open patching (F(2,22) = 24.371, p<0.001, partial η2=0.689).
source: The contrast sensitivity of the UPE becomes smaller for both of the two monocular deprivation conditions (for eye-closed patching, F(2,22) = 17.213, p<0.001, partial η2=0.610; for eye-open patching, F(2,22) = 24.371, p<0.001, partial η2=0.689; one-way repeated-measures within-subjects analysis of variance [ANOVA]), while the contrast sensitivity of the PE becomes larger or does not change (for eye-closed patching, F(2,22) = 0.447, p=0.645, partial η2=0.039; for eye-open patching, F(2,22) = 5.267, p=0.014, partial η2=0.324; one-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The contrast sensitivity of the PE becomes larger or does not change after 2.5 hr of monocular patching for eye-closed patching (F(2,22) = 0.447, p=0.645, partial η2=0.039) and eye-open patching (F(2,22) = 5.267, p=0.014, partial η2=0.324).
source: The contrast sensitivity of the UPE becomes smaller for both of the two monocular deprivation conditions (for eye-closed patching, F(2,22) = 17.213, p<0.001, partial η2=0.610; for eye-open patching, F(2,22) = 24.371, p<0.001, partial η2=0.689; one-way repeated-measures within-subjects analysis of variance [ANOVA]), while the contrast sensitivity of the PE becomes larger or does not change (for eye-closed patching, F(2,22) = 0.447, p=0.645, partial η2=0.039; for eye-open patching, F(2,22) = 5.267, p=0.014, partial η2=0.324; one-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was significant difference in contrast sensitivity ratio changes between two time points after deprivation (F(1,11) = 20.245, p<0.001, partial η2=0.648).
source: The results showed that there was significant difference between two time points (F(1,11) = 20.245, p<0.001, partial η2=0.648), no difference between two patching conditions (F(1,11) = 0.811, p=0.387, partial η2=0.069), and significant interaction of time point and condition (F(1,11) = 9.271, p=0.011, partial η2=0.457).
evidence: Supported by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claim: There was no difference in contrast sensitivity ratio changes between two patching conditions (F(1,11) = 0.811, p=0.387, partial η2=0.069).
source: The results showed that there was significant difference between two time points (F(1,11) = 20.245, p<0.001, partial η2=0.648), no difference between two patching conditions (F(1,11) = 0.811, p=0.387, partial η2=0.069), and significant interaction of time point and condition (F(1,11) = 9.271, p=0.011, partial η2=0.457).

claim: There was significant interaction of time point and condition for contrast sensitivity ratio changes (F(1,11) = 9.271, p=0.011, partial η2=0.457).

evidence: Supported by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claim: The contrast sensitivity ratio changes between the eye-open and eye-closed patching at 0' was significantly different (p=0.023).
source: Post hoc Bonferroni test showed that the contrast sensitivity ratio changes between the eye-open and eye-closed patching at 0' was significantly different (p=0.023, Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by post hoc Bonferroni test shown in Figure 4b.

claim: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, binocular perceived phase changed from –0.196±0.215° before patching to –14.196±3.184° immediately after removal of the patch.
source: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, binocular perceived phase changed from –0.196±0.215° (mean ± SE) before patching to –14.196±3.184° immediately after removal of the patch.
evidence: Measured from binocular phase combination task.

claim: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-closed condition, binocular perceived phase changed from –0.214±0.308° to –6.357±1.962°.
source: In contrast, in the PE-closed condition, binocular perceived phase changed from –0.214±0.308° to –6.357±1.962°.

source: This means that the change in sensory eye dominance, as reflected by the binocular perceived phase, was 56.1% less in the PE-closed condition than that in the PE-open condition.

claim: The binocular perceived phase significantly varied from baseline to post-measure sessions for eye-closed patching (F(3.022,39.509)=7.126, p<0.001, partial η2=0.354).
source: One-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA showed that the binocular perceived phase significantly varied from baseline to post-measure sessions: for eye-closed patching, F(3.022,39.509)=7.126, p<0.001, partial η2=0.354; for eye-open patching, F(5,65) = 11.420, p<0.001, partial η2=0.468.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of experimental data.

claim: The binocular perceived phase significantly varied from baseline to post-measure sessions for eye-open patching (F(5,65) = 11.420, p<0.001, partial η2=0.468).

evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the change of the perceived phase was significantly different between eye-open and eye-closed patching conditions (F(1,13) = 10.265, p=0.007, partial η2=0.441).
source: A two-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA also showed that the magnitude of the change of the perceived phase was significantly different between these two patching conditions (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed): F(1,13) = 10.265, p=0.007, partial η2=0.441; the interaction between patching condition (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed) and the post-measure sessions (i.e., from 0' to 30') was not significant: F(4,52) = 1.553, p=0.201, partial η2=0.107, indicating the different patching impacts between the eye-open and eye-closed patching was consistent within 30 min after the removal of the patch.
evidence: Supported by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claim: The interaction between patching condition and post-measure sessions was not significant for perceived phase changes (F(4,52) = 1.553, p=0.201, partial η2=0.107).
source: A two-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA also showed that the magnitude of the change of the perceived phase was significantly different between these two patching conditions (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed): F(1,13) = 10.265, p=0.007, partial η2=0.441; the interaction between patching condition (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed) and the post-measure sessions (i.e., from 0' to 30') was not significant: F(4,52) = 1.553, p=0.201, partial η2=0.107, indicating the different patching impacts between the eye-open and eye-closed patching was consistent within 30 min after the removal of the patch.
evidence: Supported by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claim: The different patching impacts between the eye-open and eye-closed patching was consistent within 30 min after the removal of the patch.
source: A two-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA also showed that the magnitude of the change of the perceived phase was significantly different between these two patching conditions (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed): F(1,13) = 10.265, p=0.007, partial η2=0.441; the interaction between patching condition (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed) and the post-measure sessions (i.e., from 0' to 30') was not significant: F(4,52) = 1.553, p=0.201, partial η2=0.107, indicating the different patching impacts between the eye-open and eye-closed patching was consistent within 30 min after the removal of the patch.
evidence: Inferred from the non-significant interaction between patching condition and post-measure sessions.

claim: There was a significant difference in average perceived phase change between eye-open and eye-closed conditions (t(13) = –3.276, p=0.006).
source: A two-tailed paired samples t-test also showed that there was a significant difference between these two conditions: t(13) = –3.276, p=0.006.
evidence: Supported by paired samples t-test analysis.

claim: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, the eye dominance ratio changed from 0.946±0.035 before patching to 0.459±0.061 immediately after removal of the patch.
source: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-open condition, the eye dominance ratio changed from 0.946±0.035 (mean ± SE) before patching to 0.459±0.061 immediately after removal of the patch.

claim: After 2.5 hr of monocular patching in the PE-closed condition, the eye dominance ratio changed from 0.922±0.042 to 0.508±0.075.

source: This means that the change in sensory eye dominance, as reflected by the binocular rivalry, was 6.9% less in the PE-closed condition than that in the PE-open condition.

source: One-way repeated-measures within-subjects ANOVA also showed that the eye dominance ratio significantly varied from baseline to post-measure sessions: for eye-closed patching, F(5,65) = 17.047, p<0.001, partial η2=0.567; for eye-open patching, F(5,65) = 34.987, p<0.001, partial η2=0.729.

evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the eye dominance ratio shift was significantly different between the two patching conditions (F(1,13) = 5.256, p=0.039, partial η2=0.288).
source: The magnitude of the eye dominance ratio shift was also significantly different between the two patching conditions: F(1,13) = 5.256, p=0.039, partial η2=0.288, without significant interaction between patching condition (i.e., eye-open vs. eye-closed) and the post-measure sessions (i.e., from 0' to 30'): F(4,52) = 2.009, p=0.107, partial η2=0.134 (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA).

claim: There was no significant interaction between patching condition and post-measure sessions for eye dominance ratio (F(4,52) = 2.009, p=0.107, partial η2=0.134).

claim: There was a significant difference in eye dominance ratio change between eye-open and eye-closed conditions (Z=–2.103, p=0.035).
source: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test also showed that there was a significant difference between two conditions: Z=–2.103, p=0.035.

claim: The differences in brain states between eyes open and closed could be explained by the contrasting dynamics of GABA.
source: The differences that we found in brain states could be explained by the contrasting dynamics of GABA, which has implications in interpreting MRS measurements (Kurcyus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on GABA dynamics.

claim: In complete darkness, GABA concentration decreases after eye opening.
source: In complete darkness, GABA concentration decreases after eye opening (Kurcyus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: GABA has been shown to be correlated with changes in sensory eye dominance following short-term monocular deprivation.
source: GABA has been shown to be correlated with changes in sensory eye dominance following short-term monocular deprivation, where resting GABA concentration decreases after deprivation and this decrease in GABA correlates with the individuals' binocular changes (Lunghi et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Resting GABA concentration decreases after short-term monocular deprivation.
source: GABA has been shown to be correlated with changes in sensory eye dominance following short-term monocular deprivation, where resting GABA concentration decreases after deprivation and this decrease in GABA correlates with the individuals' binocular changes (Lunghi et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The decrease in GABA after short-term monocular deprivation correlates with individuals' binocular changes.
source: GABA has been shown to be correlated with changes in sensory eye dominance following short-term monocular deprivation, where resting GABA concentration decreases after deprivation and this decrease in GABA correlates with the individuals' binocular changes (Lunghi et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: GABA can mediate neuroplastic change in primary visual cortex through long-range cortical fibers that connect large basket cells in the superficial cortical layers of the same and opposite ocular domains.
source: Animal models have confirmed that GABA can mediate the neuroplastic change in primary visual cortex through a long-range cortical fibers that connect the large basket cells in the superficial cortical layers of the same and opposite ocular domains (Buzás et al., 2001; Sengpiel et al., 1994), and short-term monocular deprivation effects are associated with reduced GABAergic inhibition in layer 4 of V1 (Reynaud et al., 2018; Tso et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to animal model studies.

claim: Short-term monocular deprivation effects are associated with reduced GABAergic inhibition in layer 4 of V1.
source: Animal models have confirmed that GABA can mediate the neuroplastic change in primary visual cortex through a long-range cortical fibers that connect the large basket cells in the superficial cortical layers of the same and opposite ocular domains (Buzás et al., 2001; Sengpiel et al., 1994), and short-term monocular deprivation effects are associated with reduced GABAergic inhibition in layer 4 of V1 (Reynaud et al., 2018; Tso et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deprivation with the PE open is expected to reduce GABA levels more compared to deprivation with the PE closed.
source: Therefore, the most parsimonious explanation is that deprivation with the PE open is expected to reduce GABA levels more compared to deprivation with the PE closed, and thus induce more changes in sensory eye dominance as a result of short-term deprivation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on previous findings about GABA dynamics.

claim: Having the eye open under the patch will result in an enhanced short-term effect for ocular dominance due to the internal neural state associated with a reduction of alpha inhibition.

claim: Depriving the amblyopic eye for 2.5 hr can strengthen the amblyopic eye's contribution in binocular viewing.
source: In fact, studies have suggested that depriving the amblyopic eye for 2.5 hr can strengthen the amblyopic eye's contribution in binocular viewing (Zhou et al., 2013b), and repeated daily short-term monocular deprivation of the amblyopic eye not only can recover visual acuity of the amblyopic eye but lead to a more balanced binocular vision in adult amblyopes (Lunghi et al., 2019c; Zhou et al., 2019), which imply that monocular patching could have sustained therapeutic benefits to be implemented as a means to rebalance the visual system of amblyopic patients and improve their monocular acuity.
